paper_metadata.title: Social deprivation and 1-year survival after stroke: a prospective cohort study

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: The study uses a prospective multicenter design across diverse geographic regions (mainland France and Overseas Departments). Inclusion/exclusion criteria are clearly defined, and baseline characteristics are thoroughly reported for both deprived and non-deprived groups.

items.label: Source of target population
items.prompt: The source population or population of interest is adequately described for key characteristics (LIST).
items.evidence_snippet: one in mainland France (Dijon, Burgundy) and five in French Overseas Departments (Fort-de-France, Martinique; Pointe-à-Pitre, Guadeloupe; Cayenne, Saint Laurent du Maroni, and Kourou, French Guiana).
items.reasoning: The study clearly identifies the geographic and clinical source of the population.

items.label: Method used to identify population
items.prompt: The sampling frame and recruitment are adequately described, including methods to identify the sample sufficient to limit potential bias (number and type used, e.g., referral patterns in health care)
items.evidence_snippet: 1573 consecutive patients were included in the INDIA study
items.reasoning: Consecutive recruitment in acute stroke units minimizes selection bias.

items.label: Recruitment period
items.prompt: Period of recruitment is adequately described
items.evidence_snippet: Between June 2011 and October 2014
items.reasoning: The specific dates for the recruitment window are provided.

items.label: Place of recruitment
items.prompt: Place of recruitment (setting and geographic location)  are adequately described
items.evidence_snippet: admitted for acute stroke... in any one of the six participating French centers
items.reasoning: The clinical setting (acute stroke admission) and specific locations are detailed.

items.label: Inclusion and exclusion criteria
items.prompt: Inclusion and exclusion criteria are adequately described (e.g., including explicit diagnostic criteria or “zero time” description).
items.evidence_snippet: Patients aged > 18 years admitted for acute stroke (ischemic stroke, spontaneous intracerebral hemorrhage or subarachnoid hemorrhage)... Patients with a history of symptomatic stroke or other short-term life-threatening diseases were not included
items.reasoning: Clear age, diagnosis, and clinical exclusion criteria are provided.

items.label: Adequate study participation
items.evidence_snippet: Not found in text
items.reasoning: The paper does not explicitly state the number of eligible patients who declined to participate (participation rate), though it mentions 1573 were included.

items.label: Baseline characteristics
items.prompt: The baseline study sample (i.e., individuals entering the study) is adequately described for key characteristics (LIST).
items.evidence_snippet: Table 2: Baseline characteristics of patients with ischemic stroke according to deprivation status
items.reasoning: Extensive baseline data including age, sex, BMI, comorbidities, and stroke severity (NIHSS) are provided.

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: The study achieved very high follow-up rates by utilizing both telephone contact and the National Identification Register for those who could not be reached, minimizing the risk of attrition bias.

items.label: Proportion of baseline sample available for analysis
items.prompt: Response rate (i.e., proportion of study sample completing the study and providing outcome data) is adequate.
items.evidence_snippet: Information on deprivation was available for 1540 (99%) patients.
items.reasoning: The study reports nearly complete data for the primary exposure and follow-up.

items.label: Attempts to collect information on participants who dropped out
items.prompt: Attempts to collect information on participants who dropped out of the study are described.
items.evidence_snippet: For patients lost to follow-up, the National Identification Register of Individuals was contacted.
items.reasoning: The authors used a national registry to verify survival status for those not reachable by phone.

items.label: Reasons and potential impact of subjects lost to follow-up
items.prompt: Reasons for loss to follow-up are provided.
items.evidence_snippet: Not found in text
items.reasoning: While they mention using a registry for those lost, they do not explicitly list the reasons for initial loss to follow-up.

items.label: Outcome and prognostic factor information on those lost to follow-up
items.prompt: Participants lost to follow-up are adequately described for key characteristics (LIST).
items.evidence_snippet: Not found in text
items.reasoning: There is no comparison table between those lost to follow-up and those who completed the study.

items.prompt: There are no important differences between key characteristics (LIST) and outcomes in participants who completed the study and those who did not.
items.evidence_snippet: Not found in text
items.reasoning: The text does not provide a statistical comparison of completers vs. non-completers.

risk_of_bias_assessment.label: Study Attrition Summary
risk_of_bias_assessment.prompt: Loss to follow-up (from baseline sample to study population analyzed) is not associated with key characteristics (i.e., the study data adequately represent the sample) sufficient to limit potential bias to the observed relationship between PF and outcome.

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: The prognostic factor (social deprivation) was measured using the EPICES score, a validated multidimensional tool. The measurement was standardized across all participants and had very little missing data.

items.label: Definition of the PF
items.prompt: A clear definition or description of 'PF' is provided (e.g., including dose, level, duration of exposure, and clear specification of the method of measurement).
items.evidence_snippet: The EPICES score is composed of 11 binary questions with a focus on marital status, health insurance status, economic status, family/social support and leisure activity
items.reasoning: The tool and its components are explicitly defined.

items.label: Valid and Reliable Measurement of PF
items.prompt: Method of PF measurement is adequately valid and reliable to limit misclassification bias (e.g., may include relevant outside sources of information on measurement properties, also characteristics, such as blind measurement and limited reliance on recall).
items.evidence_snippet: EPICES score validated on a French cohort of 197,389 subjects... shown to be a reliable tool to measure individual deprivation
items.reasoning: The authors cite specific validation studies for the instrument used.

items.prompt: Continuous variables are reported or appropriate cut-points (i.e., not data-dependent) are used.
items.evidence_snippet: patients with a score ≥ 30.17 considered as deprived [16].
items.reasoning: The cut-point used was pre-specified based on previous validation literature, not derived from the current dataset.

items.label: Method and Setting of PF Measurement
items.prompt: The method and setting of measurement of PF is the same for all study participants.
items.evidence_snippet: Specially trained clinical research technicians collected all data prospectively
items.reasoning: Standardized data collection by trained staff was used for all participants.

items.label: Proportion of data on PF available for analysis
items.prompt: Adequate proportion of the study sample has complete data for PF variable.
items.evidence_snippet: Information on deprivation was available for 1540 (99%) patients.
items.reasoning: 99% completion rate is excellent.

items.label: Method used for missing data
items.prompt: Appropriate methods of imputation are used for missing 'PF' data.
items.evidence_snippet: A complete case analysis was done when the rate of missing data was lower than 5%.
items.reasoning: Imputation was not used; however, missingness was only 1%, making complete case analysis acceptable.

risk_of_bias_assessment.label: PF Measurement Summary
risk_of_bias_assessment.prompt: PF is adequately measured in study participants to sufficiently limit potential bias.

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: The outcome (all-cause mortality) is objective and was assessed through standardized follow-up and verified against a national registry, minimizing measurement bias.

items.label: Definition of the Outcome
items.prompt: A clear definition of outcome is provided, including duration of follow-up and level and extent of the outcome construct.
items.evidence_snippet: The primary outcome was survival at 12 months, defined as the time from stroke until death from any cause.
items.reasoning: The outcome and timeframe are clearly defined.

items.label: Valid and Reliable Measurement of Outcome
items.prompt: The method of outcome measurement used is adequately valid and reliable to limit misclassification bias (e.g., may include relevant outside sources of information on measurement properties, also characteristics, such as blind measurement and confirmation of outcome with valid and reliable test).
items.evidence_snippet: Survival was determined by follow-up, including contacting a next of kin or the patient's physician... For patients lost to follow-up, the National Identification Register of Individuals was contacted.
items.reasoning: Death is an objective outcome, and the use of a national register ensures high reliability.

items.label: Method and Setting of Outcome Measurement
items.prompt: The method and setting of outcome measurement is the same for all study participants.
items.evidence_snippet: Follow-up phone calls (or visits if the patient was still hospitalized) took place 1, 6 and 12 months after stroke.
items.reasoning: The follow-up schedule was standardized for the entire cohort.

risk_of_bias_assessment.label: Outcome Measurement Summary
risk_of_bias_assessment.prompt: Outcome of interest is adequately measured in study participants to sufficiently limit potential bias.

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: The study accounted for major confounders including age, stroke severity (NIHSS), and comorbidities. It specifically addressed the violation of the proportional hazards assumption by using a piecewise model, which is a robust statistical approach.

items.label: Important Confounders Measured
items.prompt: All important confounders, including treatments (key variables in conceptual model: LIST), are measured.
items.evidence_snippet: included age, sex, body mass index (BMI), ethnic origin, home ownership, hypertension, diabetes, hypercholesterolemia, chronic heart failure, alcohol, smoking, atrial fibrillation, prior transient ischemic attack, prior myocardial infarction, pre-stroke treatment... admission NIHSS score and thrombolysis.
items.reasoning: A comprehensive list of clinical and demographic confounders was collected.

items.label: Definition of the confounding factor
items.prompt: Clear definitions of the important confounders measured are provided (e.g., including dose, level, and duration of exposures).
items.evidence_snippet: Stroke severity at admission was assessed using the National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale (NIHSS) score. The degree of disability/dependence before stroke was measured with the premorbid modified Rankin Scale (mRS).
items.reasoning: Major clinical scales are defined, but definitions for others like 'smoking' or 'alcohol' are less detailed.

items.label: Valid and Reliable Measurement of Confounders
items.prompt: Measurement of all important confounders is adequately valid and reliable (e.g., may include relevant outside sources of information on measurement properties, also characteristics, such as blind measurement and limited reliance on recall).
items.evidence_snippet: Specially trained clinical research technicians collected all data prospectively, with the assistance of the doctors responsible for patient management.
items.reasoning: Data collection by trained staff using validated scales (NIHSS, mRS) supports reliability.

items.label: Method and Setting of Confounding Measurement
items.prompt: The method and setting of confounding measurement are the same for all study participants.
items.evidence_snippet: Specially trained clinical research technicians collected all data prospectively
items.reasoning: Standardized prospective collection was applied to all.

items.label: Method used for missing data
items.prompt: Appropriate methods are used if imputation is used for missing confounder data.
items.evidence_snippet: Otherwise, a category 'missing data' was generated for the concerned covariate.
items.reasoning: The study used a 'missing category' for BMI, which is less ideal than multiple imputation but transparently reported.

items.label: Appropriate Accounting for Confounding
items.prompt: Important potential confounders are accounted for in the study design (e.g., matching for key variables, stratification, or initial assembly of comparable groups).
items.evidence_snippet: All analyses were stratified on the center for accounting potential center effects.
items.reasoning: Stratification by center was used in the design/analysis.

items.prompt: Important potential confounders are accounted for in the analysis (i.e., appropriate adjustment).
items.evidence_snippet: Multivariable Cox models were generated... Variables associated with survival at 12 months with a p value < 0.20 in the univariate analysis... were included
items.reasoning: Multivariable adjustment was performed for key prognostic factors.

risk_of_bias_assessment.label: Study Confounding Summary
risk_of_bias_assessment.prompt: Important potential confounders are appropriately accounted for, limiting potential bias with respect to the relationship between PF and outcome.

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: The statistical methods were sophisticated, including supremum tests for proportional hazards and piecewise modeling. Sensitivity analyses confirmed the robustness of the findings.

items.label: Presentation of analytical strategy
items.prompt: There is sufficient presentation of data to assess the adequacy of the analysis.
items.evidence_snippet: Survival between groups was plotted using the Kaplan−Meier method and compared using the log-rank test stratified on the center.
items.reasoning: The analytical steps are clearly laid out.

items.label: Model development strategy
items.prompt: The strategy for model building (i.e., inclusion of variables in the statistical model) is appropriate and is based on a conceptual framework or model.
items.evidence_snippet: Candidate variables for multivariable analysis were based on clinical relevance... stepwise selection procedure
items.reasoning: The model building combined clinical expertise with statistical selection.

items.prompt: The selected statistical model is adequate for the design of the study.
items.evidence_snippet: In case of violation of this assumption, a piecewise constant HR was calculated over distinct periods
items.reasoning: The use of piecewise Cox models appropriately addressed the non-proportionality of the deprivation variable.

items.label: Reporting of results
items.prompt: There is no selective reporting of results.
items.evidence_snippet: Analyses were conducted separately for ischemic stroke and spontaneous intracerebral hemorrhage
items.reasoning: Results for both stroke types and both time periods (early vs. late) are reported, including non-significant findings.

risk_of_bias_assessment.label: Statistical Analysis and Presentation Summary
risk_of_bias_assessment.prompt: The statistical analysis is appropriate for the design of the study, limiting potential for presentation of invalid or spurious results.
